title: International Finance, Lesson 4: FX risk in the accounts - transaction, translation and economic
subtitle: Three different exposures, and why only one of the three actually costs the business money
whyItMatters: A company reporting hundreds of billions in FX losses is a headline every reporting season, but most of those losses come with no cash leaving the building at all. Telling the three exposures apart is what lets you know which loss to worry about and which one is only a translation entry.
openingQuestion: A company reports an FX loss from revaluing a foreign currency loan at period end. Which exposure is this?
openingOptions: Transaction exposure, and the loss will turn into real cash
Translation exposure - a bookkeeping conversion that never touches cash flow
Economic exposure, reflecting a decline in the firm's long-run competitive position
None of them, since a period-end revaluation is only a mandatory accounting step
explanation: A foreign currency loan is a real obligation, repayable in real foreign currency. The period-end revaluation has not moved any cash yet, but it records in advance an amount that becomes cash on the repayment date unless the rate reverses. So this is transaction exposure, and it is quite different from the difference that arises when a foreign subsidiary's accounts are translated - the second kind only changes a number on paper.

diagram.label: Transaction: a real obligation in foreign currency
Only the first reliably becomes cash

realWorldExample.company: Power and airline companies with long-dated foreign currency debt
realWorldExample.description: Capital-intensive businesses often borrow in foreign currency because the rate is lower and the tenor longer. Every reporting period that loan is revalued at the closing rate, producing very large FX gains or losses in the income statement - while their revenue is almost entirely in local currency. Profit therefore swings with the exchange rate rather than with the business, and an analyst has to separate the two before the real trend becomes visible.

quiz.question: Where does translation exposure come from?
options: From converting a foreign subsidiary's financial statements on consolidation
From purchase and sale contracts settled in foreign currency
From the company holding cash across several currencies
From the spread between the buying and selling rates quoted by a bank
quiz.explanation: This difference is normally posted to a separate reserve within equity rather than through the income statement, and it only turns into cash if the business sells or liquidates that foreign investment. Contracts settled in foreign currency are transaction exposure, because they carry a real obligation on a known date. Holding balances in several currencies is a position rather than a translation effect, and the bid-offer spread is a dealing cost, not an exposure at all.

quiz.question: What is economic exposure?
options: The effect of the exchange rate on receivables already recognised in the period
The effect of currency movements on competitiveness and future cash flows
The effect of the exchange rate on the value of imported inventory in the warehouse
The effect of the exchange rate on the interest cost of foreign currency borrowings
quiz.explanation: This is the most dangerous kind because no accounting line records it. A business with no foreign currency debt and no imports at all can still lose market share when the real exchange rate appreciates and imported goods become cheaper. The other three options all describe amounts that already sit somewhere in the accounts - receivables, inventory, interest cost - which makes them transaction exposure and therefore visible, measurable and hedgeable.

quiz.question: What is the most effective natural hedge against currency risk?
options: Buying a forward contract against every foreign currency obligation as it arises
Holding a large share of assets as deposits spread across several currencies
Matching the currency of revenue with the currency of costs and debt
Moving every sales contract onto settlement in the local currency instead
quiz.explanation: A natural hedge costs nothing and carries no basis risk. An exporter borrowing in foreign currency to fund working capital is matching its own cash flows - which is why the same foreign currency loan can be prudent for one company and reckless for another. Blanket forward cover costs money and leaves basis risk behind, spreading deposits across currencies adds exposure rather than removing it, and pushing counterparties onto local currency settlement usually just moves the risk into the price they will accept.

quiz.question: When a set of accounts shows a large FX loss, what is the first thing to do?
options: Strip it out of profit, because every FX loss is a paper entry with no cash effect
Rebuild the whole forecast at whatever the rate happened to be on the closing date
Compare the size of the loss against peer companies over the same period
Work out whether it came from revaluing a real obligation or from translation
quiz.explanation: The two sources lead to opposite conclusions. Revaluing a foreign currency loan is a forecast of cash that will be lost in future; the translation difference on a subsidiary's accounts is not. The FX note in the financial statements tells you exactly which is which. Stripping out every FX loss discards the ones that matter most, a closing-date rate is one observation rather than a forecast, and a peer comparison is meaningless until the composition of each company's loss is known.

quiz.question: Why does an FX loss from revaluing a foreign currency loan matter even though no cash has moved?
options: Because it records in advance the part that becomes real cash on the repayment date
Because the loss reduces the operating cash flow the business generates in the period
Because the loss is deductible when the corporate tax charge is computed
Because it forces the company to repay the loan early under the loan agreement
quiz.explanation: The revaluation simply recognises early what is already true: the obligation is payable in foreign currency and the rate has moved. That is quite different from the translation loss on a foreign subsidiary, which sits in equity and may never become cash at all. It does not touch operating cash flow, which is computed before financing items; the tax treatment varies by jurisdiction and is a consequence rather than a reason; and no ordinary loan agreement accelerates on a revaluation.

practicePrompt.question: A company earns all of its revenue in local currency and carries a large foreign currency loan. Which statement is true?
options: The company is naturally hedged, since the two sides of the balance sheet offset
The company has large transaction exposure and profit will swing with the rate
The risk is minor, since the loan is only revalued once, on the repayment date
The company has translation exposure only, because the loan sits on the balance sheet
practicePrompt.explanation: This is the worst exposure structure there is: the obligation is in foreign currency, the capacity to repay is in local currency, and nothing offsets. When analysing a company shaped like this, compute profit before FX differences separately to see the real business trend, and run an adverse rate scenario against the ability to service the debt.

keyTakeaways: Transaction exposure attaches to a real obligation in foreign currency - it will become cash
Translation exposure is only the conversion of a subsidiary's accounts, normally posted to equity
Economic exposure appears in no accounting line but affects future cash flows
Naturally hedging by matching the currency of revenue, costs and debt is the cheapest protection available

summary.keyIdea: Not every FX loss is money lost, but the one attached to a real obligation is
summary.commonMistake: Lumping every FX difference together and then either ignoring all of it or worrying about all of it
summary.action: Find the FX note of a company with foreign currency debt and separate the revaluation part from the realised part.

application.title: Splitting profit into two parts
application.message: For a company carrying large foreign currency debt, always compute profit before FX differences alongside reported profit. The first shows the business, the difference shows the exposure - and those two stories deserve to be judged separately.
application.secondary: This is also how experienced management teams present results to investors.

sections.text: Every reporting season brings headlines about companies posting heavy losses on the exchange rate. Sometimes that is a serious warning about the ability to service debt; sometimes it is a translation entry and nobody lost anything. Telling the two apart is what this lesson is about.

sections.title: Three kinds of currency exposure
sections.subtitle: One move in the exchange rate, three very different consequences

concepts.def: A real obligation or claim in foreign currency: a loan, a payable to a foreign supplier, an export receivable. It will become cash.
Arises on converting a foreign subsidiary's accounts into the reporting currency. Normally posted to equity, and only becomes cash on disposal.
The effect of the exchange rate on competitiveness and future cash flows. No accounting line records it, and it is often the largest of the three.

left.label: The FX loss worth worrying about
left.text: The revaluation of a foreign currency loan at a company earning local currency revenue. It forecasts a larger cash outflow at repayment.

right.label: The FX loss worth less concern
right.text: The translation difference on a subsidiary that is trading steadily with no disposal planned. No cash flow changes at all.

sections.label: The most dangerous kind is the invisible one
sections.text: Economic exposure appears on no line of the financial statements, yet it can exceed the other two combined. A company with no foreign currency debt and no imports can still lose market share to imported goods as the real exchange rate moves - exactly the mechanism from the lesson on purchasing power parity.

lines: End of the stage: the exchange rate governs today's forward price, the long-run trend, the valuation model and the financial statements.
What all four lessons share is a single discipline: always know which currency you are measuring in.
